item.title: Israeli Arabs seek record turnout to oust Netanyahu in tightly fought vote
item.description: Arab parties could hold the balance of power in Israel's October 27 election as voters seek action on violent crime and discrimination under Netanyahu's far-right government ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: Israeli Arabs say the last four years under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right government have become so intolerable that they are looking to turn out in record numbers to unseat him. It’s a shift for the demographic, who make up about 20 per cent of the population, as they’ve often stayed at home on election day in opposition to a political system they say excludes them. The outcome could be to make two main Israeli Arab parties the kingmakers in what’s expected to be an extremely tight vote on October 27. “They ignore us, they attack us, they incite against us, but we’ll be the October surprise and we will send this evil government home,” Ahmad Tibi, the leader of the Ta’al party, told supporters at a packed rally in Tel Aviv earlier this month. “The situation is dangerous and unprecedented.” Party and community leaders, including United Arab List head Mansour Abbas, cite open discrimination by government officials as having got worse during Netanyahu’s latest term as leader. That includes a failed attempt to stop Arab parties from running in the election. Police neglect in the face of surging violent crime in Arab communities has also worsened, Abbas has said — especially since the October 2023 Hamas attacks that triggered the war in Gaza. There were 252 homicides in Israeli Arab towns in 2025, the deadliest year on record, with 182 more in the year to date, according to Abraham Initiatives, a Jewish-Arab NGO. “It’s an emergency we haven’t seen in the past, this extremist, messianic government,” Mahdi Kabaha, an Arab Israeli lawyer and voter from the north of the country, said by phone. “This government doesn’t want us Arabs as citizens.” Turnout among Israeli Arabs, who are Israeli citizens as opposed to Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza, could reach about 70 per cent, Tibi predicted, compared with 53 per cent at the 2022 election. That could deliver 13 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, according to an October 10 poll by the public broadcaster Kan, up from 10 in the outgoing parliament. Most mainstream Israeli parties have ruled out partnering with an Arab party in any future coalition government. But if neither Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc nor the Opposition under Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar is able to clinch a 61-seat majority — as polling suggests — discussions are likely to take place. Eisenkot has said he’ll not accept a party that doesn’t acknowledge Israel as a Jewish state or won’t recognise Hamas as a terrorist organisation that must be dismantled. That would exclude the Joint List, a three-party bloc of which Ta’al is part, although not the United Arab List, the second main option. Netanyahu’s party, Likud, has used the possibility of Eisenkot partnering with Arabs as an attack line designed to play on fears of another October 7-style attack, warning in a recent campaign video that the vote posed a choice between “the Right or Palestine.” The Joint List is aiming for 10 seats — enough to edge out other small, right-wing parties and influence the nature of the next government. The group’s leader, Yousef Jabareen, said it could act as a “safety net” to a new government — giving support from outside the coalition. The United Arab List has said it is willing to participate in government directly, as it did briefly in 2021. That party, led by Abbas, is also aiming for 10 seats. The combined 20 would, if the targets are met, outperform the polls. A recent survey conducted by the Konrad Adenauer Program for Jewish-Arab Cooperation found that more than 77 per cent of Israeli Arabs want to see an Arab party inside government. Their main priority is to address violent crime that has been sweeping Arab communities, according to 71 per cent of respondents. Meanwhile, only 8 per cent said their vote would hinge on resolving the longstanding issue of the establishment of a Palestinian state. That polling suggests most Israeli Arabs want to pick up where they left off in 2021, when the United Arab List, also known as Ra’am, joined a short-lived governing coalition under Prime Minister Naftali Bennett — a historic first for an Arab party. During that period, Abbas focused on directing government funding to Arab towns rather than advancing a peace deal for Palestinians, which was then — and even more so now — seen as unlikely. Abbas secured a multi-year, 30-billion-shekel ($9.8 billion) investment aimed at narrowing the gap in education, housing and healthcare between Arab and Jewish communities — an initiative halted by Netanyahu’s government when it took power in 2022. With the help of then-deputy national security minister Yoav Segalovich, Abbas has said he slashed violent crime in Arab communities by 10 per cent. Ahead of this year’s vote, Abbas has appointed Segalovich — a Jewish official — as his deputy. In a recent election campaign video set to a triumphant soundtrack, he appealed to voters to build on the achievements of his initial time in government, and “in three years, four years, completely end the violence and crime phenomenon.” He’s also accepted Israel as a Jewish state. The desire for more influence comes as Israeli Arabs become more integrated into institutions such as hospitals — making up a quarter of all doctors in the country — and expand their presence in tech, finance and other sectors. In 2004, the first Israeli Arab permanently joined the Supreme Court; in 2019, the first Israeli Arab became the head of one of Israel’s largest banks. Yet as Israeli society has grown more right-wing, even affluent Arabs have reported discrimination when buying apartments in Jewish-majority neighbourhoods, according to Adalah, a legal organisation for Arab minority rights in Israel. They are sometimes barred by admission committees which, under Israeli law, are able to vet applicants based on their “compatibility with the socio-cultural fabric of the community,” said the group, which unsuccessfully petitioned the Supreme Court to overturn the law in 2011. There’s also been a surge in the demolition of unauthorised structures in the Arab sector, with more than 14,000 homes and infrastructure razed since 2023 in the Negev, in southern Israel, driven by intensified government enforcement, according to Adalah. Many Arab villages and towns lack adequate sewage, transport, schools and housing infrastructure — while being blighted by gang violence. Israeli Arabs still want to see a Palestinian state, said Khalid Ghanaim, a lifelong Ra’am voter from Sakhnin, an Arab town in northern Israel that’s seen a spate of shootings. “But there’s another view that’s becoming more popular, which is that a person needs to eat, to be safe, in order to stand up for their principles,” he said. “That political involvement is a question of survival.” This election is the first since the October 7 attacks, the deadliest in Israeli history, in which Hamas militants killed 1,200 people and abducted 250 more — including Israeli Arabs. At least 74,000 people have been killed in Israel’s war against Hamas in Gaza, according to the Hamas-run health ministry in the territory. That conflict has been in a state of tenuous ceasefire for about a year, and the territory has been largely destroyed by Israel’s bombardment. “There’s a sense that this government is leading a total war against Palestinians, wherever they are,” said Raef Zreik, a legal expert at the Van Leer Institute, a research centre in Jerusalem. All Arab parties have said they will unite to remove ministers like Itamar Ben Gvir, a once-fringe politician who advocates for the annexation of Gaza and the West Bank. Last month, Netanyahu and Ben Gvir sought to bar the participation of Arab parties, alleging they support terrorism against Israel. The parties denied the claims and the petitions were overturned by the Supreme Court. Aida Touma-Suleiman, an Israeli Arab lawmaker from the Joint List, said the disqualification efforts sought to strip Arabs of their right to vote — but had instead encouraged her base. “We hear it in the streets this time, that everyone needs to go out and vote,” said Touma-Suleiman. “This time, we are going to get rid of them.”

item.title: France reels after riots leave one dead, over 2,000 arrested nationwide
item.description: Riots over high prices and declining public services damaged hundreds of shops and injured more than 600 police officers, as Macron prepared to address the nation on Sunday ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / France reels after riots leave one dead, over 2,000 arrested nationwide

France reels after riots leave one dead, over 2,000 arrested nationwide Riots over high prices and declining public services damaged hundreds of shops and injured more than 600 police officers, as Macron prepared to address the nation on Sunday

Fire in Limoges city hall amid protests, in Limoges, France, October 17, 2026, in this screengrab from a video obtained from social media. Lucas Destrem/via Reuters

Reuters Paris 4 min read Last Updated : Oct 18 2026 | 9:29 PM IST

Listen to This Article

France reeled on Sunday from one of its most violent days of unrest in years after protests over high prices and public services left one demonstrator dead, thousands arrested and hundreds of police injured.   Nationwide demonstrations erupted into riots on Saturday, with a town hall torched, shops ransacked and buildings covered in graffiti as violent groups clashed with police in cities across the country.   One protester died after suffering a cardiac arrest during demonstrations in Paris. Police made more than 2,000 arrests across France, while more than 600 officers were injured, the interior minister said.   "It's like a war zone here," said Dutch entrepreneur Tije De Boer, who had come to Paris with his children to visit a friend and said the protests forced him to evacuate his hotel at Place de la Republique, a trouble hotspot on Saturday.

More than half a million people joined marches in scores of cities, marking the convergence of a month-long student movement with broader social discontent over rising living costs and declining public services. Also Read

Mass demonstrations in France spiral into worst violence in decades

Cyberattack targets French supermarket fridges, sparks fires, spoils food

France confers highest civilian honour on Bharti Enterprises' Sunil Mittal

Why are thousands of French students protesting across the country?

France plans trials of AI-powered 'wingmen' for Rafale jets by 2028

President Emmanuel Macron will address the nation at 8 pm local time (1800 GMT) on Sunday, his office said.   Saturday's unrest laid bare the deep anger at Macron, who leaves office in 2027 after a decade in power that has increasingly become defined by social discontent, a weak economy and ballooning debt.   The government has blamed the violence on hard-left and ultra-left groups, as well as criminals who it said instigated the looting.

Several hundred shops damaged   While hundreds of thousands protested peacefully, violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, looted luxury boutiques and supermarkets, and attacked police vehicles and officers.   A massive clean-up operation began in cities from Lille in the north to Marseille in the south and Strasbourg in the east to Bordeaux in the south-west, where a masked mob invaded the residence of the local prefect.   Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said several hundred shops had been damaged on Saturday.   In Paris, smashed shop windows, burnt-out bicycles and spray-painted slogans bore witness to a day that began largely with peaceful demonstrations but descended into violence.   In Limoges, south-western France, Mayor Guillaume Guerin denounced the chaos after the city's 143-year-old town hall was set ablaze and largely destroyed in an arson attack on Saturday, drawing comparisons to the 2019 fire that devastated Paris's Notre-Dame Cathedral.

"There was a clear, premeditated intention to burn down the town hall, and the people inside feared for their lives," Guerin told Reuters. He threatened to resign if the city did not receive the funds needed to repair the town hall.   Presidential election to take place next year   The unrest has increased pressure on President Macron and his government ahead of a presidential election due next year.   Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu blamed the unrest on the "ultra-left" and criminals.   Economy Minister Roland Lescure pledged support on Sunday for business owners who suffered losses. "Those who break things will pay, repair the damage and be held accountable for their intention to sow chaos," Lescure said in a statement.

Bordeaux Mayor Thomas Cazenave said up to 100 stores had been looted in his city, while Marseille Mayor Benoit Payan announced emergency financial aid to support those businesses affected by the violence.   French retailer Carrefour's CEO Alexandre Bompard told French broadcaster BFMTV that 50 of the company's shops had been damaged, including 20 that were looted, with losses from the damage running into the tens of millions of euros.   The protests began last month over school conditions and teacher shortages in working-class suburbs, before broadening into a movement against inequality, public spending cuts and the rising cost of living.   More From This Section

item.title: IMF-World Bank meetings leave developing nations short of fresh answers
item.description: Developing countries face rising debt costs, inflation and AI risks, but the Bangkok meetings ended without new initiatives, leaving familiar fiscal advice and uncertainty ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / IMF-World Bank meetings leave developing nations short of fresh answers

IMF-World Bank meetings leave developing nations short of fresh answers Developing countries face rising debt costs, inflation and AI risks, but the Bangkok meetings ended without new initiatives, leaving familiar fiscal advice and uncertainty

International Monetary Fund (IMF) Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva speaks during the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank Group in Bangkok, Thailand, Friday, Oct. 16, 2026.(Photo:PTI)

Reuters Bangkok 5 min read Last Updated : Oct 18 2026 | 9:19 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Last week's meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank yielded no new answers for the developing world to the questions posed by a spreading West Asia war, continuing war in Ukraine, rising debt payments and a potential AI bubble.   Not for the first time, lower-income countries are being rocked by the spillover from the actions of wealthier nations: rising debt service costs, higher inflation and the risk of falling ever further behind economically thanks to the AI boom.   What they got was the stock advice the global lenders always dish out: to shrink fiscal deficits and accelerate economic reforms to attract more private sector investment.

Kristalina Georgieva, the first IMF chief from a developing nation — Bulgaria — said advanced economies were in fact the worst offenders on budget imbalances. She noted that developing countries' debt levels had actually fallen in recent years, only for surging bond yields elsewhere to drive up their borrowing costs.   Average debt service payments there had more than doubled from a decade ago to 14 per cent of government revenue, crowding out education, healthcare and other critical areas, she said. Also Read

AI risks may outweigh benefits without safeguards, warns IMF chief

India's WPI inflation may breach 12%, retail 6% in October: Ind-Ra

Wholesale inflation hits series high of 11.39% in September on broad rise

Wholesale inflation jumps to 11.39% in September as food, fuel costs rise

Tamil Nadu overtakes Telangana with highest retail inflation in September

Advanced economies focused on their own problems   At a panel on Saturday, Georgieva said many issues remained unresolved, especially around AI:   "We are in a place where we have many more questions than we have answers. And my alert to everybody is: Do not fall for the guys that pretend they have the answers. They are tricking you." Josh Lipsky, vice-president of international economics at the Atlantic Council think tank, said the meetings had missed their opportunity to come up with guidance or ways to help.

"It's hard to talk about the developing world when the advanced economies don't have their act together and are at risk of a fiscal crisis," he said. "And that's on top of political situations in many of these countries that makes development aid not a priority at the moment."   Mauricio Cardenas, Colombia's former finance minister and now a research scholar at Columbia University's School of International and Public Affairs in New York, said many policymakers were left with a deep sense that "something really bad could happen" but no real roadmap to navigate the future.   "The IMF and World Bank are not particularly well prepared for this new phase. They understand that something is going on, they bring in experts on AI," he said. "But in the end, there's no kind of specific, concrete advice on how to be prepared for something where you don't really understand how it's going to unfold."

The geopolitical tensions that have roiled both institutions since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 — complicating concerted action — were also evident in Bangkok when nearly half the delegates at an IMF steering committee walked out when Russia's finance minister spoke.   Houthi attacks on Riyadh airport delayed the arrival of the head of that committee, Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed Al-Jadaan, who had to travel overland to Qatar to catch a flight.   And Bangkok itself was a stark reminder of the challenges facing developing countries, still partly under water after floods in September that caused almost $200 million in damage to Thailand's industrial sector.

Rising inequality could raise costs in long term   Kate Pickett, a professor at the University of York, urged policymakers to focus on more inclusive growth rather than forcing developing countries into tough structural reforms.   "If inequality increases, if poverty deepens, that will increase their costs in the long term," she said. "It's not enough to describe an economy as resilient. It's only resilient for the rich and the privileged."   Ayhan Kose, deputy chief economist at the World Bank, said the global economy had weathered its biggest energy shock — from the US-Israeli war on Iran — better than expected.   But while a global recession had been avoided, he said growth outlooks in both developing and advanced economies were worse than before.

Growth had already fallen off in half of advanced economies, while in developing countries as a whole, it had slowed significantly to around 3.6 per cent from 4.4 per cent.   “People are really worried because resilience today is not a guarantee for resilience tomorrow," he said. "Now they are worried about what will be the next shock, because every six months, if not every three months, there is a new shock." While no specific initiatives were announced, he said the World Bank remained focused on helping developing countries prepare for advancements in AI, in part by mobilising more private capital, now at triple the levels of 2022.

Yet it, too, has to contend with sharp drops in official development aid and persistent challenges in attracting foreign investment to developing countries.   “The reality on the ground is the reality on the ground,” he said.

item.title: Blaze at St Petersburg oil sites as Kyiv launches drones at Russia
item.description: Ukrainian attacks set an oil export terminal ablaze in St. Petersburg on Sunday, as Kyiv launched more than 1,000 drones across Russia in one of its largest ever aerial bombardments.
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / Blaze at St Petersburg oil sites as Kyiv launches drones at Russia

Blaze at St Petersburg oil sites as Kyiv launches drones at Russia The attack comes amid deepening tensions between Ukraine and Washington, with U.S. President Donald Trump criticizing Kyiv for its strikes on Russian oil infrastructure

Plumes of smoke rise from fires (centre) at an oil refinery following what the authorities say is a Ukrainian drone strike in the course of the Russia-Ukraine conflict | REUTERS

AP Moscow 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 18 2026 | 4:03 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Ukrainian attacks set an oil export terminal ablaze in St. Petersburg on Sunday, as Kyiv launched more than 1,000 drones across Russia in one of its largest ever aerial bombardments. The attack comes amid deepening tensions between Ukraine and Washington, with U.S. President Donald Trump criticizing Kyiv for its strikes on Russian oil infrastructure. One person was killed and five more were wounded in the attack, which sparked fires at both the Petersburg Oil Terminal and the city's Ruchi oil depot, said local Gov. Alexander Beglov. A logistics center belonging to Russian retailer Ozon and a data center for local tech giant VK were also targeted, both companies confirmed.

Russia's Ministry of Defense said Sunday that its forces had destroyed 1,015 Ukrainian drones over 15 Russian regions, as well as the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black Sea. Meanwhile, a woman died and at least two other people were wounded, including a 6-year-old girl, after Russia launched two attacks on the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia, local officials said. Also Read

How geopolitical stigma associated with Putin is affecting Russians

Many don't know what my decision is: Trump on Russia sanctions waiver

Trump wants 60 days to analyse impact of Russia sanctions law: Rubio

Two apartment buildings, 18 cars and an educational institution were damaged as a result of the attack, head of the Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration Mykhailo Semikin said. Russia continues energy attacks, Kyiv says US President Donald Trump announced on Oct. 11 that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" in the 4 1/2-year-old war, but offered no details on it and Kyiv reported attacks by Moscow on energy sites after his statement.

Ukraine confirmed Thursday it had resumed attacks on Russian oil after a three-day hiatus. Zelenskyy was outraged by Russia's continuing aerial bombardment of his country's energy infrastructure in apparent defiance of Trump's demand on Sunday for both sides to halt those attacks. The Ukrainian government initially said that it was heeding the ceasefire. In a post on X Sunday, Zelenskyy said that in the week since Trump's announcement of an energy ceasefire, Russia had attacked Ukraine's energy, oil and gas sectors 76 times. He also said that in the past night alone, energy facilities in four Ukrainian regions had been attacked and tens of thousands of families were still without power. He accused Russia of trying to cause a blackout.

"America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements. On the contrary, they take every signal of an opportunity to make money as proof that their bet on war is paying off and they can keep fighting," he wrote. Zelenskyy also stressed that the war was continuing due to Russia's invasion - not because Ukraine was defending itself. "It is Russia that must face pressure for peace to have a chance. Thank you to everyone who understands this and helps," he said.

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)
